slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: In the sentence “Fishes swim,” the subject is “Fishes” and the predicate is “swim.”
There is no separate copula — no word like “are” is expressed.
One word can affirm something of a subject directly, expressing both the copula and the predicate.
A word used in this way — to affirm action, being, or state — is called a Verb.

slides.text: A Verb is a word which expresses action, being, or state.

slides.heading: Every Sentence Needs a Verb
bullets: The verb is the word that tells what the subject does or is.
Cross out the verb and the sentence falls apart:  “The dog ___ the ball.”
Ex. — Birds sing.   The sun shines.   Children laugh.   Water freezes.
Ex. — Mother bakes bread.   The team won.   Flowers are pretty.
In each one, the underlined-in-your-mind action or being word is the verb.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Verb
slides.instruction: Name the verb in each sentence.  (Just find it — don't worry about its class yet.)

slides.heading: Transitive Verbs
bullets: A Transitive Verb requires an object to complete its meaning.
The object receives the action of the verb.
Ex. — Columbus discovered America.   Maria painted the fence.   The dog buried a bone.
Test — ask “verb + what?”  If there is an answer, it is transitive:  “discovered what? America.”
Rem. — The object is not always written out:  “The child reads.”  (reads what? — understood.)

slides.heading: Intransitive Verbs
bullets: An Intransitive Verb needs no object to complete its meaning.
The action stops with the subject; nothing receives it.
Ex. — Horses run.   The baby smiled.   Snow falls.   The engine hummed.
Test — ask “verb + what?”  If there is no answer, it is intransitive:  “run what? — nothing.”
Rem. — Many verbs can be either:  “She reads books” (transitive) or “She reads well” (intransitive).

slides.heading: Copulative (Linking) Verbs
bullets: A Copulative Verb joins a predicate to the subject and makes an assertion.
It links the subject to a word that describes or renames it.
Ex. — Lambs are playful.   The weather was warm.   The soup tastes good.
Common linking verbs — am, is, are, was, were, seem, become, feel, taste, look.
The copula is always a verb.

slides.heading: The Three Classes at a Glance
bullets: Transitive — passes the action to an object:   Dogs chase cats.
Intransitive — the action has no object:   Dogs bark.
Copulative — links the subject to a describing word:   Dogs are loyal.
Notice: the same subject can take all three — it all depends on the verb.

slides.instruction: Split each sentence into subject | predicate | object.  Remember: the divider after the subject reaches below the baseline.

slides.heading: Common Mistakes with Verbs
bullets: Use seen and gone only with a helper (has, have, had):  “I have seen it,” not “I have saw it.”
Use saw and went by themselves for past time:  “I saw a horse,” not “I seen a horse.”
Say did and came — not done and come — for past time:  “He did his work.”  “Father came home.”
With two or more subjects, use are or were:  “The horse and the cow are in the stable.”
With the subject you, always use were:  “You were there,” not “You was there.”

slides.heading: Practice — Fix the Verb
slides.instruction: Each sentence has a verb mistake. Give the correct word.
items: I have saw a fine horse today.
He done his work well yesterday.
The horse and the cow is in the stable.
My father come home last week.
I seen John at the fair.
George has went there several times.
What three things can a verb express?
Is a transitive verb's object always written out?
answers: A word that expresses action, being, or state.
One that needs an object to complete its meaning.
One that needs no object to complete its meaning.
One that links a predicate to the subject and makes an assertion.
No — “The child reads.”  (reads what? — the object is understood.)
Only with a helping verb — has, have, or had.
